claims.text: Business finance is the money a business raises and uses to pay for what it needs before, or faster than, its own trading income can pay for it; the need arises because spending and earning do not line up in time.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Start-up finance pays for what has to be in place before the first sale: premises and deposits, equipment, opening inventory, registration and licence fees, and the rent, wages and power of the trading months before the business covers its own costs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Growth is paid for before it pays: extra capacity, extra inventory and extra staff are bought and paid for in the months before the higher sales they make possible are received, which is why a business can be growing quickly and short of money at the same time.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business that is trading and profitable can still need finance to survive, because the money it owes to suppliers, staff and lenders falls due on fixed dates while the money owed to it by customers arrives on the customers' timetable.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Survival needs arise from events outside the business plan - a fall in demand, a customer paying late, a breakdown, a rise in the cost of supplies - and each is a demand for money at a moment when trading has not produced it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A short-term need for finance is one the business expects to settle within about a year, arising from day-to-day trading: paying for inventory, wages, fuel and overheads in the weeks before the customers who will fund them have paid.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A long-term need for finance lasts more than about a year, arising from spending on assets and capacity - vehicles, machinery, premises, a new production line - that will be used, and will earn revenue, over several years.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The matching principle holds that finance should be repayable over a period similar to the life of the need it pays for: finance repayable in months against an asset earning over years puts the repayments ahead of the earnings, while finance repayable over years against a need that lasts weeks leaves the business paying for something long after it has gone.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Whether a need is short or long term is decided by how long the money stays tied up before trading returns it, not by the size of the amount: a large sum needed for six weeks is a short-term need and a smaller sum committed to a machine for seven years is a long-term one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Profit is what is left of a period's revenue once the costs of earning that revenue are taken off, so profit = revenue - costs; it is recorded when a sale is made and when a cost is incurred, not when money moves.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cash is the money a business actually holds - in the bank and in the till - and can pay with today.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Credit trading separates the two figures: a sale made on credit is added to profit when the goods are delivered but adds nothing to cash until the customer pays, and a cost paid in advance leaves the bank before it is charged against profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Two further movements take cash without reducing the profit of the period by the same amount: repaying borrowed money returns finance rather than paying a cost of trading, and buying a non-current asset takes the cash in full on the day of payment while its cost is spread across the years the asset is used.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business can report a profit in a period in which its bank balance falls, and can hold plenty of cash in a period in which it makes a loss - for example after selling an asset or receiving new finance, neither of which is revenue.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The two figures answer different questions: profit answers whether trading added value over a period, and the cash balance answers whether the business can pay what falls due now.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Failure from lack of finance follows a self-reinforcing sequence: an amount falls due that the business cannot pay, unpaid suppliers tighten credit or ask for cash with order, stock must then be paid for before it is sold, staff whose wages are late leave, customers move their orders, and in the end a creditor takes legal action and a formal insolvency procedure begins.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The immediate cause of a formal insolvency procedure is an inability to pay an amount that has fallen due, which is a cash failure; a business can reach that point with a full order book and profitable products.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Bankruptcy is a legal declaration that a person cannot pay their debts as they fall due; control of that person's assets passes to an appointed official, the assets are sold, and the proceeds are shared among the creditors in an order set by law.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Bankruptcy reaches business owners through unlimited liability: because a sole trader or ordinary partner is not legally separate from the business, its debts are that person's own debts and creditors may pursue assets held outside the business, such as a house, a vehicle or savings.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For an owner declared bankrupt the loss is not limited to what was put into the business, and the personal consequences of the declaration, such as restrictions on borrowing or on holding certain offices, attach to the person and outlast the business.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Liquidation, also called winding up, is the process by which a company is brought to an end: an appointed liquidator takes control, sells the company's assets, pays the proceeds to creditors in an order set by law, distributes anything remaining to shareholders, and the company then ceases to exist.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Compulsory liquidation is forced on a company, typically after an unpaid creditor applies to a court for an order, while voluntary liquidation is begun by the company itself through its shareholders, which may follow an inability to pay debts and may also happen for reasons unconnected with insolvency, such as owners closing a solvent business on retirement.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because a company has limited liability the creditors' claims in a liquidation stop at the company's own assets, so shareholders lose what they invested but their personal assets are not normally reached; a debt a shareholder or director has personally guaranteed is a separate personal obligation and can still be enforced.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Administration is a procedure in which a company in financial difficulty is placed under the control of an appointed insolvency practitioner, who takes over the running of it from the directors in order to rescue the company as a going concern, or failing that to obtain a better result for the creditors as a whole than immediate closure would produce.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: What makes the rescue attempt possible is time: while a company is in administration it normally has protection from creditors enforcing their claims, so the administrator can sell the business as a working whole, renegotiate what is owed, close loss-making parts or find a buyer, instead of the business being dismantled piecemeal.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Administration is temporary: it ends when the company is handed back in a workable state, or sold, or when the attempt fails and the company passes into liquidation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The three procedures differ on who they are about and what they are trying to achieve: bankruptcy concerns a person who cannot pay and realises that person's assets; liquidation concerns a company and ends it; administration concerns a company and attempts to save it, so the business may survive.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The precise legal procedures and the names given to them differ from one country to another, so what the syllabus requires is the difference of purpose between the three rather than the law of any single jurisdiction.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Working capital is the finance a business has available for its day-to-day operations, measured as current assets minus current liabilities and expressed as a sum of money.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities, where current assets are cash plus the items expected to become cash within a year - inventory and trade receivables - and current liabilities are the amounts payable within a year, such as trade payables, an overdrawn bank balance, tax due and unpaid wages.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Working capital is needed because of a gap in time between paying for inventory and labour and being paid by customers; the longer that gap, the more money has to stand behind it, and it is what allows a business to meet obligations on the day they fall due rather than on the day its customers pay.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Too little working capital starts a sequence that feeds itself: suppliers paid late tighten terms or ask for cash with order, so stock must be paid for before it is sold, prompt-payment discounts are lost, staff whose wages are late may leave, and inventory may have to be sold quickly at a reduced price, each step leaving less money for the month after.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Too much working capital carries an opportunity cost, because money held in inventory and in unpaid customer accounts earns nothing while it sits there and inventory held a long time may be damaged, become unsaleable or pass its date; the aim is enough to meet what falls due with as little as possible tied up beyond that.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A working capital figure is interpreted by setting it against the payments the business must make and by looking at what it is made of, because a positive figure composed mostly of inventory and receivables does not show that the business can pay a bill this week.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Trade receivables are amounts customers owe the business for goods or services already delivered on credit, and trade payables are amounts the business owes suppliers for goods and services already received on credit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Managing trade receivables runs through a sequence of decisions: checking a customer before granting credit and setting a limit, stating the payment terms on order and invoice and applying them consistently, invoicing promptly and accurately, using a schedule of overdue accounts to decide which to chase first, and deciding what to do about persistent late payers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Every decision about receivables trades cash against sales: tighter credit, shorter terms and firmer chasing bring money in sooner but may cost the order, while generous credit wins sales and ties up more money in accounts that are not yet paid.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Trade payables are a source of day-to-day finance that carries no interest, so using the full agreed credit period rather than paying early keeps money in the business; paying beyond the agreed period is different, because a supplier whose money is late may shorten the terms, ask for payment with order, withdraw a discount or decline to supply.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Receivables and payables pull on the same cash: money is tied up while customers owe the business and released while the business owes its suppliers, so the shorter the collection period and the longer the payment period - within what has been agreed - the less working capital the business has to find elsewhere.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A discount offered for early payment is a certain cost incurred on every account that takes it, set against a saving that lasts only as long as the money would otherwise have been outstanding, so the two are compared over the same period before the offer is judged worthwhile.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Capital expenditure is spending on non-current assets - items bought to be kept and used in the business for more than a year, such as vehicles, machinery, premises, computers and fixtures - including the cost of getting them installed and working.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Revenue expenditure is spending on running the business day to day and used up within the period it is incurred: wages, rent, fuel, raw materials, insurance, power, advertising and routine repairs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: What decides the classification is what is bought and how long it will be used, not how much it costs: a delivery van is capital expenditure and a year's insurance on the same van is revenue expenditure, and a repair that keeps an asset doing what it already did is revenue expenditure while an addition giving it a new capability for years is capital expenditure.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Revenue expenditure is charged in full against the profit of the period in which it is incurred while capital expenditure is not, because the asset is used over several years and its cost is spread across them, so two businesses spending the same cash in a month can report different profits.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Capital expenditure ties money up for years and is therefore a long-term need for finance, while revenue expenditure recurs each period and is released as customers pay, which makes it a short-term need carried by working capital.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Buying a non-current asset reduces the bank balance by the full amount on the day it is paid for while reducing that period's reported profit by much less, so a business reading only the profit figure can approve a purchase it can justify and still be unable to pay its wages at month end.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
